newsitem.title: TAIWAN: "King share" Asustek wants more than boards.
newsitem.headline: "King share" Asustek wants more than boards.

text.p: With profit margins three times the level of other Taiwan motherboard makers, Asustek Computer Inc says it expects to post 1996 earnings per share of T$33 (US$1.2) -- the highest among all Taiwan shares.
Taiwan's personal computer industry, the world's third largest, is renowned for its makers' flexibility and quick response to global trends.
Asustek says its ambition is to spur new trends.

"While other local motherboard makers define their business as assembly, we define ours as marketing strategy and design our products to make the market accept our products," vice-chairman T.H. Tung told Reuters in a recent interview.
"In addition to assembly-line profits, we create profits by setting market segments and innovating product design."

Asustek forecast 1996 pretax profit of T$4 billion (US$145 million) on sales of T$13.4 billion (US$487 million), a profit margin of some 30 percent against most other Taiwan motherboard makers' 10 percent margins, Tung and securities analysts said.
The 1996 forecast was up from Asustek's 1995 pretax profit of T$2.057 billion (US$75 million) on sales of T$7.873 billion (US$286 million).
Tung attributed Asustek's success to its advanced technology and intensive cooperation with Intel Corp, whose market-leading Pentium chips form the heart of its boards.

Such cooperation enabled Asustek to be first to market with motherboards for Intel's 486 and Pentium chips and this, in turn, enabled Asustek's customers to be first to market with Pentium computers, he said.

The industry's short life cycle -- two years product life and dwindling profits after six months on the market -- had forced Intel to work with suppliers right from the start of new product development, Tung said.
Intel liked Asian suppliers' flexibility, he said.

"Intel prefers East Asian partners instead of large U.S. firms, as the latter tend to have their own development strategy, and this gives Taiwan computer makers a chance to have such a fast development," Tung said.
Despite its success in motherboards, Asustek has ambitions to step into other product lines, Tung said.
"Asustek is not limited to motherboard production. Our vision is to produce any add-on-value products in the computers, communications and consumer electronics industries," he said.
Asustek is now developing integrated services digital network (ISDN) products and computer servers.
"We will also introduce personal data assistants, notebook computers and network management software in 1997," Tung said.
"We love to play new products."
Analysts praised Asustek's past performance and forecast its success will continue through 1997.

"Asustek products often revolutionise the price/performance of the PC systems. With this competitive advantage, the company can charge more than a 20 percent premium over its competitors," said David Chang, an analyst at Grand Cathay Securities.

"Due to the volume shipment of Intel's Pentium Pro systems that started in the fourth quarter of 1996 and the production ramp-up of its facility, Asustek, we expect, should sustain its growing momentum through 1997," Chang said.
Grand Cathay is forecasting Asustek's 1997 earnings per share at T$33.5 (US$1.22).
Analysts also expect the price of Asustek shares, which debuted on November 14 at T$108, to rally to T$300 or above.
Asustek already has captured the stock market's "king share" title for the share with the highest price, surpassing Cathay Life Insurance on November 21.
Showing no signs of slowing, Asustek rocketed the daily seven percent limit for the ninth consecutive session on November 23 to end at T$194.

"Since the share price of an electronic company is capable of reaching 10 times its earnings-per-share, Asustek is looking at a share price that could soar to T$320," said Michael Hung, head of research at Nikko Securities.
Nikko forecast 1996 earnings-per-share at T$32 for Asustek, the highest ever for a listed electronics share.
Analysts expect Asustek, the island's number three maker of motherboards, to turn out three million units in 1996 and five million in 1997.
"We haven't made an annual output forecast, but since we now have a monthly production capacity of 450,000 motherboards, their estimates are reasonable," Tung said.
